title: Ludwigia perennis: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Ludwigia perennis in Rice Fields: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Ludwigia perennis, or sigang dagat, is a short kahoy kahoy weed of lowland palay. Learn to spot its yellow flowers and the beetle that eats it.
excerpt: Ludwigia perennis is a short, yellow flowered broadleaf weed that farmers call Kahoy kahoy, malapako, tina tina or sigang dagat. It grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it among its look alike cousins and how to control it before it spreads.

heroImage.alt: Perennial water primrose (Ludwigia perennis), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Dinesh Valke from Thane, India, CC BY SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
In English, Ludwigia perennis is called perennial water primrose. It is part of the evening primrose family, Onagraceae. Farmers call it Kahoy kahoy, malapako, tina tina or sigang dagat. The first three names are shared with other Ludwigia weeds, so check the flowers closely. Being a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. Its English name says perennial, but the plant grows as an annual and finishes its life in one season. It spreads by seed and also by plant fragments. Broken pieces left on wet soil can grow into new plants. So rough weeding that leaves pieces behind can spread it further.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Ludwigia perennis
rows: Kahoy kahoy, malapako, tina tina, sigang dagat
Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look for a small, upright, branched plant up to 30 cm tall. The stems have uneven ridges and are sometimes reddish. Its leaves are narrow and lance shaped. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The yellow flowers have four or five egg shaped petals. Then count the stamens. They match the number of sepals, unlike the eight stamens of its bigger cousins. The seed pods have four angles and are reddish.

items: Short, upright, branched plants no taller than about 30 cm.
Stems with uneven, irregular ridges, sometimes with a reddish tinge.
Narrow, lance shaped leaves growing along the stems and branches.
Yellow flowers with four or five egg shaped petals.
Look alike tip: it has as many stamens as sepals, while seedbox and Mexican primrose willow have eight.
Reddish seed pods with four angles forming after the flowers drop.

blocks.text:
This weed is small, but it still takes a share of what your palay needs. It competes with rice for water, fertilizer and light, most of all while the rice is young and short. When many plants grow close together, the rice hills get crowded and grow weaker.

Because it spreads by seed and by plant fragments, careless weeding can make it worse. Broken pieces left in the mud can root again. Plants that set seed also fill the soil with seed for the next cropping. Some seed caught at harvest can end up in palay you save for planting, so the problem follows you.

blocks.title: Its weak spot
blocks.text: A leaf beetle works on your side against this weed. The Altica beetle, from the chrysomelid family, feeds on it. Both its larvae and adults eat the leaves hungrily. When you find these beetles chewing kahoy kahoy leaves, leave them alone and avoid spraying insecticide there. They weaken the weed for free while you handle the rest.

items: Pull whole plants with their roots and bring them out of the paddy, because broken fragments left in the mud can grow again.
Weed before the flowers turn into reddish seed pods, since plants that set seed fill the soil for next season.
Spare the Altica beetles you see eating its leaves, and avoid insecticide sprays where they feed.
Because it stays short, it can hide below the rice leaves, so check low between the hills when you walk the field.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Ludwigia perennis down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Ludwigia perennis Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Ludwigia perennis

items.q: What is this weed called in Tagalog and other local names?
items.a: Farmers call it Kahoy kahoy, malapako, tina tina or sigang dagat. Its English name is perennial water primrose. The first three local names also cover other Ludwigia weeds, such as seedbox and Mexican primrose willow. To be sure, look for a short plant with yellow flowers and as many stamens as sepals.

items.q: How do I control it in a rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field. Keep shallow water where you can, and hand weed early, pulling whole plants so no fragments stay behind. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label, and spare the Altica beetles that eat it.

items.q: Is Ludwigia perennis really an annual if its name says perennial?
items.a: Yes. The English name can confuse farmers, but this weed grows as an annual and finishes its life in one season. It comes back through the seeds it drops and through plant fragments left after weeding. So the way to stop it is to keep it from setting seed and to clear the broken pieces.
